en: Preface to the *Cautionary Admonition* (Jingce) of Mount Gui: When a person first descends to earth, are they truly so shrouded in obscurity? Or is there perhaps that which is not so shrouded?
Ignorance leads to birth; greed and desire lead to aging; anger leads to illness; and delusion leads to death. One undergoes these...

Entrusting one’s form to nature, do not forget that it awaits its end. To emerge as a monk is to act without contravening what is required. Through cultivation, one illuminates the nature; through the nature, cultivation is initiated.
When abiding in the nature, cultivation is entirely perfected within the nature; when abiding in cultivation, the nature is entirely perfected within cultivation.

Nevertheless, those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom strip away the sand to find the treasure, while those of middling or inferior capacity merely count the grains of sand. As the Sūtra says: "If a bhikṣu, though..."

Those who uphold the prohibitive precepts yet, for the sake of gain and support, associate with those who have broken the precepts, sharing their worldly occupations—these are called the "mixed monks" (*saṃkīrṇa-saṃgha*).

Or, those who dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*) but are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not desire to beg for alms, who see only what is not kin, and are unable to provide instruction—these are called the "foolish monks" (*bāla-saṃgha*).
Furthermore, it is said that their original nature is pure and cannot be defiled by hundreds of thousands of millions...

He is one who can withstand the obstructions and destruction wrought by various māras, and is able to discipline the two aforementioned groups, causing them all to dwell securely in the supreme realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
He is thus an unsurpassed guide for the protection of the Dharma. Looking back through the ages, was not the Great Master Daoyuan of Damei the very person?

Setting aside the fact that mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is his essence and responding to conditions is his function, his fame resounded across the two mountains and his Way was transmitted to thousands.

The "Ancient" refers to the single text of the *Jingsi* (Exhortation). Like a mani jewel of five colors, it benefits both the ordained and the laity alike, encompassing both the great and the small vehicles.

It is universally esteemed for its monastic discipline and earnestly practiced as the profound Way. (I, the unworthy,) have frequently expounded upon it and have now once again annotated and explained it, desiring that all sentient beings throughout the world may realize that the mundane world is like a dream and understand that phenomena are unborn, thereby together upholding the ancestral style of Baizhang and deeply attaining the state of extinguished embers.
A small fire; an ancient path with broken steles. Where patterns give rise to the flame of wisdom, the water-buffalo before the mountain returns home at its own pace.
Though it is said that this is but a temporary divergence on the road, it is called "not being lost."
Composed on an autumn day in the year of Jiaxu during the Chongzhen era at Jingye Lou in Tangxi by the monk Daxiang of Jinshan,
with a commentary based on the *Jingsce* (Admonition) of Chan Master Dayuan of Mt. Miu.
Mount Gui is located in Ningxiang County of Changsha Prefecture; it is also known as Mount Daguī. It spans one hundred and forty *li*, and the Guī River originates there, hence its name.
The Chan Master’s name was Língyòu, and his posthumous title was Dàyuán. He was a native of the Zhào clan of Chángxī in Fúzhōu.
Having received the Dharma from Master Bǎizhàng, he served as the master of the refectory within the assembly. This was due to the influence of the Head Monk Sīmǎ Tóutuó.
He arrived at this mountain by chance; as soon as his mind was awakened, he kicked over the pure water jar. He resided on the mountain for more than ten years.
Later, he obtained Yangshan Huiji, with whom he together propagated and developed the Way; thus it is called the Guiyang School.
Taking the purity of one's own mind as "Chan" (Dhyāna), and taking the patterns of all phenomena as the "Master," he would warn those who were not diligent and spur those who required encouragement.
They do not advance.
For one who receives a body bound by karma cannot yet escape the encumbrance of form.
Generally speaking, the essential nature of sentient beings is fundamentally pure; it is entirely due to the non-awakening of ignorance that thoughts arise and manifest their characteristics.

Continued: Consequently, there arise delusion, karma, and afflictions, from which one cannot escape bondage. Because of this, one receives this body, which is burdened by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is the physical form inherited from one's parents, brought into being through the convergence of various conditions.

This explains how the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) enters the womb. Through the formation of inverted perceptions and the conjunction of three conditions, the physical body gradually takes shape.
These various conditions—namely, the father, the mother, and oneself, along with heat, breath, and consciousness—must all come together for birth to occur.
Although the four great elements support [the body], they are constantly in opposition.
The four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind. Regarding how these support the body while being constantly in opposition, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"Earth, water, fire, and wind together constitute the body, like four venomous snakes dwelling in a single basket. Earth and water... [and so forth].
The snake of phlegm (kapha) tends to sink downward; the two snakes of wind (vāyu) and fire (pitta) are by nature light and upward-moving. Due to these conflicting tendencies, various diseases arise.

These, in the end, all revert to the law of cessation. According to the power of their karma, they receive physical forms. Thus it is said that there are those who grasp at a self and sentient beings.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness do not wait for an appointment with anyone.
As for impermanence, there are three aspects: first, death; second, old age; and third, illness. These arrive suddenly;
how could they have a fixed limit? Furthermore, there are two kinds of impermanence: first, the impermanence of decay and destruction; second, the impermanence of every thought-moment.
Morning they exist, evening they perish; in a single *kṣaṇa*, one passes into another world.
The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "For several days. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way.
He then asked another śramaṇa, "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied, "For the duration of a meal. The Buddha said, "You..."
Not knowing the answer, he asked another śramaṇa: "In what interval does a person's life reside? He replied: "In the interval between an inhalation and an exhalation.
The Buddha said: "Excellent! You know the Way, my son. Ninety kṣaṇas constitute one thought-moment (nāṇī); within that thought-moment is a single kṣaṇa."
After nine hundred births and deaths, one will immediately be reborn in another world.
Like spring frost or morning dew, things vanish in an instant; how could trees on a riverbank or vines by a well endure for long?

Four points of meaning prove that the preceding moment differs from the subsequent world: first, it is likened to spring frost that easily melts; second, it is likened to morning dew that easily dries;
third, it is likened to a tree on a riverbank that easily collapses; fourth, it is likened to a well-rope that easily snaps. Regarding "spring frost," the ancients said:
Clear dew covers the marshy orchids; hoarfrost clings to the wild grasses. In the morning one is a handsome youth; by evening’s dusk one has become an ugly old man.
Regarding the morning dew, an ancient song says: "Dew upon the leeks—how easily it dries! Once the dew has dried, it falls again tomorrow morning.
When a person dies and departs once, when will they ever return? Regarding the trees on the bank, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "It is like [the trees] by a river..."
A tree standing on a precipice, if it encounters a violent wind, will inevitably fall over. Human beings are likewise:
when they stand on the perilous brink of old age and the gale of death arrives, they have no power to remain. Regarding the "well-vine," the Sūtra says:
It is as if a person were walking through a vast wilderness amidst a great conflagration and being pursued by a mad elephant; seeing a withered well with a tree upon it, and on that tree—
There was a vine. A man climbed the vine and suspended himself within a well. Below were three venomous dragons and four poisonous snakes;
furthermore, there were black and white rats that gnawed at the vine from all sides. There were also poisonous bees surrounding him, yet there was a small amount of honey dripping into his mouth.
Because of his greed for the honey, he forgot his suffering. Now, the "vast wilderness" refers to the triple world (*triloka*); the "tree" refers to suffering.
The body is the vine; the life-faculty is the elephant; impermanence is the murderous ghost. The black and white mice are the sun and moon;
the well is the Yellow Springs (the underworld). The three dragons are the three poisons; the four snakes are the four great elements. The honey is the five desires.
Because of greed for wealth, beauty, and other such desires, one consequently forgets the great suffering of birth and death.
Thought after thought passes with such rapidity that in a single kṣaṇa, the turning of a breath is already the next life. Why then do you remain complacent and let time pass in vain?
These four lines summarize the preceding text: first, each step is more urgent than the last; second, the four great elements are constantly in opposition;
third, impermanence does not wait for man; fourth, morning and evening, moment by moment, belong to different worlds. Fourthly:
The analogies of spring frost and morning dew illustrate this: the five [aggregates] are swift in every thought-moment, existing only within a single *kṣaṇa*.
If for even a single breath one does not turn [toward the Dharma], that is itself rebirth. How can one remain complacent and fail to attend to it, letting a lifetime pass in vain?
The preceding section up to this point is a general account applicable to both monastics and laypeople; from here on, there will be a specific account of those who have left the household life.
If parents do not provide them with delicacies, their six kin will surely abandon and distance themselves from them.
The Buddha said: "The hearts of parents extend their kindness even before form has taken shape.

From the moment of conception, for ten months, they undergo all manner of suffering and distress—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—which cannot be fully expressed by words. Even when they obtain sensual pleasures, they do not give rise to attachment."

The mind of anxious concern is never at rest. When there is difficulty in childbirth, it is as if hundreds of thousands of blades are vying to butcher and carve [the mother], ultimately leading to her death.
The grace of nurturing extends across the heavens; the thought of compassion is vast beyond compare.
Now that you have left the household life, on one hand, you are unable to provide the two Honored Ones with the finest delicacies and rich flavors; on the other—

Such a person abandons their kin—uncles, paternal cousins, aunts, and brothers—and is unable to bring peace to the state or govern the country. Their family estate is suddenly cast aside, and their lineage is severed.

"Bringing peace to the state" means leveling the world; "governing the country" means assisting a sagely sovereign. Yet they have abandoned their parents and family estate, cutting off their own progeny.
The succession of the lineage has been maintained. Fourth, one does not act [for worldly gain].

What is the intention behind this? It is to distance oneself from one's hometown and kin, shave one’s hair to receive the precepts from a teacher, diligently apply the practice of self-restraint within, and outwardly propagate the virtue of non-contention.
To be utterly detached from the mundane world and to aspire toward liberation—this is the profound intent.
A thousand two hundred and fifty households constitute a *xiang* (district), and five hundred households constitute a *dang* (clan).

These refer to the three clans of father, mother, and wife. Now, when it is said that one receives a teacher and shaves the hair, what is the purpose of this? Within, one must be diligent and self-conquering.
Eliminate the seeds and habitual tendencies; outwardly, you should propagate the virtue of patience, which is like water and milk, free from contention.
Transcend the dust and toil of kalpas beyond measure, and sever the afflictions both within and without the three realms.

How is it that as soon as one ascends to the level of the precepts, one immediately claims, "I am a bhikṣu"? One consumes the property of the Sangha as if it were one's own requirement for offerings from donors.
Merely ascending to the level of the precepts—meaning the ten precepts advance toward the two hundred and fifty—one considers oneself a bhikṣu. A bhikṣu possesses the five virtues of a *bhikṣu*:
first, his nature is supple, which is like being able to subdue the coarseness and wildness of body and speech; second, he spreads his influence like a creeping vine...

1. Cloth: This is a metaphor for transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings, continuing in an unbroken succession. 2. Threefold fragrance wafting afar: This is a metaphor for the pervasive scent of precepts and virtue, becoming known by all.
3. Able to cure various ailments: This is a metaphor for being able to sever the poisonous harms of afflictions (*kleśa*).

4. Not turning one’s back on the sun’s light: This is a metaphor for always facing the Sun of the Buddha. This is precisely what it means to look at the name and contemplate its meaning; how could one bear the title without the reality?
"Bīn" (賓) means "to receive. "Tán" (檀) means "giving" (*dāna*). "Yuè" (越) means "to transcend. Because of this great donor, one transcends that sea of poverty.
What is required consists of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine. That which is permanently established is called the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters.

They do not reflect upon the source from which [the food] comes, but say, "It is the natural law that we should share this. Having eaten, they gather together in a noisy clamor, speaking only of various worldly matters.
A bhikṣu receiving food should perform the five reflections, contemplating its source as previously described in the four [reflections].

As for material offerings, these pertain to lay bodhisattvas who, within the sphere of their own physical and verbal actions, economize on their personal sustenance to bestow gifts upon monasteries in pursuit of the fruits of merit.
As the saying goes: "When the sun is at its zenith, plowing the rice fields; sweat drips onto the soil beneath the grain.
Who knows that every grain of rice in the meal upon one's plate was earned through bitter toil? Alas, how can shameless monks speak so recklessly?
They accepted those offerings and ate their fill, gathering in pairs to discuss only matters of kings, women, and bandits;
how could they have known of the Path of Seeing, the Path of Cultivation, or the Path of Realization?
Thus, for the duration of one lifetime, people pursue pleasure without realizing that pleasure is the cause of suffering.
As for "one lifetime," it may last three months or half a year; its length is not fixed. Regarding "pleasure is the cause of suffering," the Patriarch said:
"Receiving alms is like receiving an arrow; taking food is like ingesting poison. The Buddha said:
"For example, the necessities of life required by the world can serve as causes for pleasure, yet one does not realize that they cause people to give rise to great distress.

Within birth and death, everything is suffering; there is no characteristic of pleasure. It is like a beautiful flower stalk entwined by a venomous snake. Suppose there were a person who, by nature, loved beauty..."
A flower. Not knowing that the stalk of the flower is the affliction of a venomous snake, one reaches out and grasps it. Having grasped it, one is bitten by the snake;

having been bitten, one’s life comes to an end. In the same way, ordinary persons who crave the flowers of the five sensual desires are bitten by the venomous snake of craving. When their lives come to an end, they fall into the three evil realms.
In past kalpas, you pursued the dust of the world without ever reflecting back upon yourself.
Regarding "past": *kalpa* (劫) is the name for the shortest unit of time, a *kṣaṇa* (刹那); it is also the name for the longest unit of time, a *kalpa* (劫波).
Since immeasurable kalpas past, sentient beings have followed their faculties toward the six sense objects, their minds lacking any reflection or introspection.
Thus time has been wasted and years have slipped away; while their enjoyments have been abundant and their gains and benefits have been profuse.
"Time" (shiguang) refers to the passage of time; "years and months" (suoyue) refers to the span of years. "To be submerged" (yanmo) means to waste away; "to be lost" (cuotuo) means to be indolent.
"Abundant and thick" (yinfan nonghou) refers to excessive indulgence in enjoyment.
Passing through years and decades, they do not intend to abandon or leave it behind. As their accumulations grow ever more numerous, they maintain this illusory physical form.

For many years and generations, they remain attached to it, never thinking of relinquishing it or cultivating weary detachment (*nirveda*). Thus, as they continue to accumulate and gather, it becomes increasingly abundant;
they maintain this empty and illusory body, desiring to enjoy it for a long life. Such is the folly of those lacking the nature of wisdom.

Falsely falling into stinginess and greed, the Teacher has issued a decree to exhort the bhikṣus: advance on the Path and adorn yourselves with virtue; yet there are three things that are always insufficient, and many people fall into these.
Indulging in sensory delights without ceasing, days pass and months come until, in a flash, one’s hair turns white.
The sentient beings of the six realms are submerged in the long night of birth and death; blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, they wander.

Our Buddha, the celestial sun of the Buddha-nature, shines brilliantly to draw them out from the dark alleys of ignorance; thus he is called the Guide. He issues commands and admonitions, exhorting and encouraging us. The three constants are never enough.
First is clothing: by renouncing fine ornaments, one wears garments of dyed, coarse color. Second is food: obtaining just enough to sustain the body, so as to remove hunger and thirst.
Third is sleep: practicing wholesome dharmas so as not to let the time pass in vain. Now, you have instead become addicted to these three things without ceasing;
before you know it, old age arrives, and this entire life has been wasted.
Later students have not yet heard the essential purport; they ought to consult extensively those who possess prior knowledge.

One might assume that the purpose of leaving the household life is merely to seek clothing and food, but the "purport" refers to the penetration of the fundamental principle (*zongtong*) and profound study—namely, the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

Those of later generations have not heard this and should seek out those who have attained mastery, questioning them broadly and in detail. How can it be said that one leaves the secular world to become a monk only to be preoccupied with the trivial matters of body, clothing, and mouth?
[They] merely eat. The Buddha said there are three kinds of renunciation. The inferior renunciation takes the ten precepts as its basis;
although one has abandoned one's kin, one still engages in worldly activities due to causal conditions.

The middling renunciation abandons the conditions of worldly activity and fully receives the eighty-four thousand causal conditions for tending toward the Path; yet, the actions of body, speech, and mind are not yet fully pure. The mind—

The fetters still remain; one has not yet reached the essential deliverance. Those who have gone forth as monastics possess faculties and minds that are sharp and keen; they should abandon the fetters, latent tendencies, and entanglements.
Through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, their minds attain liberation, and they emerge from the household of causal affairs and afflictions.

The Buddha first established the Vinaya to initiate and enlighten the ignorant. Its rules and dignified deportment are as pure as ice and snow; its prohibitions and observances, as well as transgressions and commissions, restrain the beginner's mind.
Through these minute regulations, all vulgar and corrupt practices are reformed.
"Vinaya" refers, for now, to the precepts of the five groups of the renunciant community: namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās.

"Initial" means that one gradually attains a virtuous model according to specific matters. Since the outward appearance was regulated before the mind was regulated, and self-restraint was not yet capable of encompassing others, it is called "initiating the ignorant.

[The *Sānqiānwēiyí* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners) and the *Bā...*] (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Sānqiānwēiyí Bǎifǎzì Jīng* [Sutra of Three Thousand Dignified Manners and Eighty Thousand Subtle Practices].)
There are ten thousand subtle practices that may be taken as models and standards, as pure as ice or snow. "Observance and maintenance" refers to the purity of the seven branches of discipline;

"commissioning and transgression" refers to the violations of the five categories of offenses. The detailed regulations and their various corruptions are fully set forth in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and other such sections.

I have never once been privileged to attend the assemblies for the Vinaya teachings, nor am I capable of discerning the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle. It is a pity that my entire life has passed in vain;
regret is difficult to undo once it has arisen.

*Vinaya* refers to the section on the monastic discipline (*vinaya-piṭaka*). "To receive the favor" means to rely [upon it]. *Nītārtha* (definitive meaning) refers to the superior vehicle’s sudden teaching, which differs from the non-definitive teachings.
"Discriminating" means to clearly distinguish and discern the doctrines and principles of the Great and Small Vehicles. If one does not practice, it is spent in vain;
at the time of death, this is called "regret."
One has never applied oneself to the principles of the teachings (*śāstra*), nor has one found any cause for awakening to the profound Way (*mārga*).
"The principles of the teachings" refers generally to the twelve divisions of the Tripitaka; "never applied oneself" means one has never settled the mind upon them.

"The profound Way" refers to the separate transmission of the mind-seal (*citta-mudrā*), the direct pointing and singular upholding; it is also what is called the Bodhisattva’s birth in the state of right nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*). One does not perceive even the slightest...

The Dharma consists in the eternal severance of habitual tendencies and entry into the Tathāgata’s omniscient wisdom; it is the realization that means both the awakening to the principle and the awakening of the mind.
Yet, as one grows old and senior in years, one may become empty-minded and arrogant, refusing to draw near to virtuous friends and knowing only how to be haughty.

"Year" refers to the year of one's birth; "lunar month" (la) refers to the seniority of one's precepts. To lose learning and exist only with an empty stomach, while harboring evil habits and a vainly exalted mind—this is what is meant.
Virtuous conduct is called "excellent" (liang); those of like mind are called "companions" (peng). Arrogance is precisely what constitutes an exalted mind.
Unfamiliar with the monastic laws (*vinaya*), they lack all sense of restraint. They speak loudly and in high voices, uttering words without moderation.

They show no respect for the senior, middle, or junior monks, treating them no differently than a gathering of Brahmins. Their bowls and alms-basins clatter as they eat; they rise before their meal is finished.

Their conduct is erratic and contrary to propriety, utterly devoid of the character of a monk. They are restless in both rising and sitting, disturbing the minds of others, and do not observe even the slightest rules of decorum.
With such minor matters of decorum, how can one restrain oneself? Future generations of new students will have no cause for emulation.
"Dharma" (law) refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras; "restraint" (戢斂) refers to body, speech, and mind. These two phrases provide a general statement, which is then detailed below:
first, speaking loudly and with a high voice; second, uttering words without regard for timing or measure; third, lacking respect.
Venerable predecessors have established that those who have received full ordination for five years are called junior seats (下座); those with ten years are called middle seats (中座);

and those with twenty years are called senior seats (上座). The *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, those who received the precepts first sit in front, and those who received them later sit behind.
Do not be like the deluded people of external paths, whose seating has no proper order; such is the law of the Brahmins."
Fourth, making noise with one’s bowl or alms-basin. Fifth, rising before others have finished eating. Sixth, coming and going in a disorderly manner, like two horns pointing in opposite directions.
Seventh, completely lacking the essence of the Sangha. The Sangha is called the "harmonious assembly.

The essence of the Sangha refers to the three meanings, the five divisions, the six harmonies, and the ten virtues. Above, it repays the fourfold debt of gratitude; below, it relieves the suffering of all living beings.

The following is a summary: All instances of agitation, haste, or causing others to harbor suspicions stem from a total lack of even the slightest adherence to the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
For those who come later and are new to the study—namely, the future members of the Dharma family—since there is no precedent to follow, why should they be bound by such constraints?

As soon as they become aware of one another, they immediately say, "I am a mountain monk. They have not heard the teachings of the Buddha regarding practice and conduct; they consistently harbor a coarse disposition.
Generally, those who are monks address themselves to others as "So-and-so" (Amuka), reserving the title "Poor Daoist" (Pindao) for great masters of knowledge alone. Or...
I am called a mountain monk. At present, I have attained a slight degree of awakening and discernment;

yet, I am unwilling to accept this title because, throughout my past life, I have not heard the principles of the Buddha. Consequently, my practice and cultivation have been coarse rather than refined, and superficial rather than matured.
Such a view arises because those at the beginning stage are indolent and gluttonous, following along with worldly habits until they have grown callous and wild.
Unaware that their feet have reached old age, they face a wall whenever they encounter matters of life.
This single phrase summarizes the preceding text. It refers to those who, having first left the household life, became habituated to indolence and gluttony, passing their days in negligence.
As time slipped away, they developed the coarse and rustic air of the wild fields;
their physical forms grew decrepit, appearing like withered bamboo drooping downward or like the legs of a crab. They were like those facing a wall, claiming they do not understand.
The principles of meaning are beyond verbal expression; it is as if one were standing with their back to a wall.

When later students come to inquire, there is no word with which to guide them; even if there were words, they would not touch upon the canonical scriptures, and one might instead be treated with contempt for speaking too lightly.
He then rebuked the junior monk for his lack of propriety; anger and resentment arose within him, and his words became offensive.
Regarding all inquiries into the principles of the Dharma, he offered no response to guide the disciple's faculties. "Dianzhang" refers to the chapters and sentences of the scriptures.
Alternatively, there may be junior students who, upon hearing such disparaging words, give rise to a heart of resentment and a fit of indignation;
yet they address the person as one of advanced age and long standing in the monastic order.
One morning he lay ill upon his bed, entangled and oppressed by manifold sufferings. From dawn until dusk he brooded over them, his heart filled with agitation;
the path ahead was vast and obscure, and he knew not where it would lead.
The manifold sufferings refer to the decline of illness, the decline of old age, the decline of wealth, and the decline of kin. To be "distraught" means to be terrified and without a master.
The "path ahead" refers to the dark journey; the five destinies are vast and boundless, with no fixed destination for where one goes.

From this point on, I have finally come to know how to repent my transgressions. What is the use of digging a well when one is already thirsty? I regret that I did not practice in advance; now that I am advanced in years, I am burdened with many faults.
Just as those living in a place without water must dig a well in advance to obtain relief, if one waits until the moment of thirst, even if one digs, what can be done?
Furthermore, if one does not prepare while practicing, then when old age arrives, there will be nothing but many faults;
at the moment of departure, one will be distracted and wavering, terrified and panicked, like a bird flying out when a window curtain is torn—consciousness follows along with karma.
When one squanders wealth at the point of departure, the signs of death manifest before them, accompanied by various terrors. The metaphor of the silk cloth refers to the illusory body;
the metaphor of the sparrow’s flight refers to the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*). The *Sūtra of the Seven Noble Women* states: "A sparrow enters a jar, and its mouth is covered with silk."
The silken gauze is torn and the magpies fly away; the conscious mind follows karma as it wanders. Regarding "the conscious mind following karma," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Cognitions and views constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts one from land to land."
It is like a person burdened by debt: the stronger creditor drags them away first. When the mind’s tendencies are manifold, it falls toward whichever is heaviest.
For example, when a debtor has many creditors, those with smaller claims must yield to those with larger ones who drag him off. Now, within the mind there are many kinds of good and evil tendencies;
it will necessarily fall first toward whichever is weightiest. As it is said: "If passionate emotions are many and wholesome thoughts few, one flows into [the realms of suffering]."
They are born perversely. With seven emotions and three thoughts, one becomes a hungry ghost; with nine emotions and one thought, one sinks down into the wheel of fire.
If the emotions are purely intense, one sinks into the Avīci Hell.
The murderous demon of impermanence does not pause for a single thought-moment; life cannot be extended, and time cannot be waited upon.
The murderous demon of impermanence means that the messengers of Yama have already arrived; one cannot linger for even a single instant, for life—does not [endure].
It may be delayed slightly, yet not even a moment’s wait is possible;

nor can wealth or power bring one to the realms of humans, devas, or the three states of existence, for one shall inevitably escape them not. To receive such a body—beyond mere calculation of kalpas—is truly a cause for lamentation and wonder.
How poignant and heart-wrenching! How could one remain silent? We must exhort one another.
"Human and celestial" refers to the vehicle of humans and the vehicle of devas. "The three realms of existence" refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
Having not yet escaped saṃsāra, how can one avoid the various destinies? Repeatedly taking up a body and then discarding it, from kalpa after kalpa—this alone is enough to evoke deep sentiment.
Alas! First, it is lamentable; second, it is pitiable; third, it is a cause for sighing; fourth, it is a cause for astonishment; fifth, it is truly tragic; sixth, it is truly heart-wrenching.
How could one remain silent with a sealed mouth? One must instead exert oneself and encourage others.

What I regret is that we were born together in this age of semblance-dharma (*sāṃprata-dharmapratirūpaka*). The time since the Sage departed is remote; the Buddha-dharma has become sparse, and many people are indolent.
"The age of semblance" refers to the final period of the semblance-dharma. Since the Sage departed, more than three thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the Three Jewels—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the appearance of these jewels in the world has become sparse. Among us humans, there is generally a lack of diligence.
I briefly extend my limited perspective to inform those who come after. If one does not eliminate self-conceit, it will truly be difficult to escape the cycle.
"Limited perspective" refers to looking at a leopard through a tube, seeing but a single spot. "Eliminate" means to cast off old habits; "self-conceit" refers to being arrogant and indolent.
"Cycle" implies revolving like a wheel, where there is an escape only when one has reached the end. This is a general statement regarding the upward path. Regarding the [preceding] direction...
The following is a specific account.
Now, as for those who have left the household life, they set out with their feet directed toward the transcendent realm; both mind and body differ from the mundane world.
It is said here that whoever becomes a monk, from the very first step, transcends all directions and, for the duration of this single life, differs from the secular world. Departing...
Having shaved off beard and hair and donned the *kāṣāya*, one’s two minds differ from the laity; afflictions are severed and eliminated while Bodhi increases.

Thus one upholds the lineage of the Sages, strikes terror into the armies of Māra, repays the four debts of gratitude, and delivers beings from the three realms of existence. If one does not act in this manner, it is a mere pretense to join the ranks of the Saṃgha.
To cause the noble lineage to flourish is to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom. For any bhikṣu, there are three occasions to strike terror into the armies of Māra:
first, upon shaving the head; second, upon generating the bodhicitta; and third, upon realizing non-arising. There are four debts of gratitude: first, the debt to one's parents;
second, the debt to sentient beings; third, the debt to the king; and fourth, the debt to the Triple Gem. To have been recklessly included among the ranks of the saṃgha is said to be...
They have left home in name only, lacking any genuine practice.

Their words and deeds are coarse and negligent, yet they vainly receive offerings from the faithful. They have not moved a single step from where they were years ago; their entire lives pass in a state of daze.
On what can one rely?
Their speech is coarse and neglectful, failing to engage with the canonical scriptures; their conduct is coarse and neglectful, never departing from worldly defilements.

They consume offerings in vain and must inevitably repay this debt. As it says below: "Though their form differs from the secular, their conduct remains as before—vague and fleeting, their appearance like that of a phantom."
If it were not for the purity of meditative concentration, how could one rely upon it?

Moreover, that these monastic forms and appearances are so dignified and worthy of admiration is entirely due to the cultivation of roots of goodness in past lives, which has brought about such extraordinary retribution.
The various fruits of the roots of goodness all arise from the practice of precepts and patience. The Buddha said:
"People in the present world see them with joy because they saw others with joy in their past lives."

If you merely intend to sit upright with hands folded, you will not value even a moment of time; your endeavors will lack diligence, and there will be no cause for the achievement of spiritual fruits.
How could you allow this life to pass in vain? Furthermore, it would provide no benefit for future karma.
Those who fold their hands [in idleness] sit and enjoy what is provided to them. An ancient saying goes: "The Sage King Yu always cherished every inch of time;
as for the common people, they should cherish every minute. This serves as a supplement. The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "Because of the power of merit and virtue, there is now much compliance;
because there is now much compliance, negligence arises. Within negligence, there is no mind of upholding the precepts. By reason of these causes and conditions..."
He entered hell.
Taking leave of his kin, he resolved to don the black robes of a monk. Reflecting day and night on what it was he sought to transcend, he thought: "How can I allow time to pass by idly?
My heart’s aspiration is to become a pillar for the Buddha-dharma, serving as a mirror for future generations. He constantly held this intention, yet was unable to [fulfill it].

Partially corresponding [to this], one parts from kin and dons the dyed robes; setting one’s resolve as the priority, one must apply the mind day and night—how could one permit even the slightest indulgence?

A vessel of great capacity will surely become a ridgepole or a beam; a vessel of small capacity serves only as a rafter or a corner-beam. As for the tortoise, it is able to determine good and ill fortune.
A mirror can serve as a standard for discerning beauty and ugliness; one who acts in such a corresponding manner is truly called a "Dharma-son.

Their speech must engage with the classical texts, and their discourse must rely upon the examination of antiquity. Their physical demeanor is exceptionally distinguished, and their spirit is lofty and detached.

The second phrase means: do not speak what is contrary to the Dharma; do not act contrary to propriety; in all conduct, one must investigate the ancient models and refrain from being a Zen practitioner who fabricates things arbitrarily.

The third phrase means: maintain the prohibitive precepts with the body, and be dignified and resolute in one’s gaze. The fourth phrase means: keep the mind fixed on meditative contemplation and abandon all clamor and distraction.
A long journey requires the assistance of good companions; one must repeatedly purify the ears and eyes. When dwelling in a place, one must choose one's associates;
from time to time, one should hear what has not been heard before. Thus it is said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who perfect me are my friends."
That which the ears hear and that which the eyes behold must depend upon virtuous friends and refined companions to purify the five turbidities and all evils.
Guan Zhong said: "Those who gave me life were my parents; those who understood me were Master Bao."
To associate with the virtuous is like walking amidst mist and dew: though they do not moisten one’s clothes, they provide occasional refreshment.
Walking through mist and dew is a metaphor for following the True Dharma; "not moistening the clothes" is a metaphor for not receiving benefit all at once;

"occasional refreshment" is a metaphor for attaining gradual benefit. The verse says: When a worthy person associates with others, it is like being permeated by incense; advancing in wisdom and practicing virtue, their conduct becomes perfected.

Those who are fragrant and pure, yet associate with the wicked, harbor biased views, and commit evil from dawn until dusk, will receive retribution even in this present life and sink into the depths after death.
Once one loses this human body, it may not be regained for ten thousand kalpas. These words of loyalty, though harsh to the ear—how could they not be engraved upon the heart?

"Evil" refers to the ten unwholesome actions, evil knowledge and views, the ninety-six types [of heterodox paths], the commission of evil, the ten causes of habitual practice, and the mutual retribution—the six modes of mutual retribution—through which one sinks into the suffering of the three miserable realms.
"Human" (ren) means benevolence; it is the heart of Heaven and Earth, the source of the Five Elements.

If the five precepts are either fully observed or partially deficient, one will never again be reborn [in such states]. Thus, the *Brahmāyu Sūtra* says: "As a lay follower of pure faith, maintain benevolence by refraining from killing;
be contented by refraining from stealing; remain chaste by refraining from sexual misconduct; uphold sincerity by refraining from deception; and fulfill filial duty by refraining from intoxication."
Loyal words are not easily entered into the ear; only the wise can take them to heart and engrave them there. The verse says: A base person is infected by others, like being near a foul object;

gradually becoming deluded and habituated to what is wrong, they do not realize they have become evil. This is a general exhortation for those above; as for those below, they must certainly practice in this manner.
One can then cleanse the mind and nurture virtue; obscure one's traces and conceal one's fame. The innate spirit is preserved within, and clamor and noise are brought to a complete halt.
The first phrase washes away the ordinary mind and nurtures sagely virtue. The second phrase obscures one’s tracks and conceals one’s reputation.
The third phrase preserves the spirit within, lest it be needlessly dissipated. The fourth phrase severs the clamor of the mundane world and returns forever to [the source].
Quiescence. If one wishes to engage in Chan and study the Way, thereby suddenly transcending the gates of expedient means:
"Chan" (禪) is translated here as *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (静虑), which is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; "the Way" (道) refers to unsurpassed Bodhi.
The Way: this Dharma does not rely on expedient means; it is the gate of direct transcendence.

When the mind accords with the profound ford, one investigates the subtle and essential, discerns the deep and abstruse, awakens to the true source, and extensively consults those who possess prior knowledge.
1. Associate with virtuous friends. 2.
First awaken to and subsequently cultivate a single phrase. 3. Thoroughly investigate the essential points of two phrases. 4. Discern and resolve the profound and abstruse meanings of three phrases.
5. Awaken to the true nature and original source through four phrases. 6. Extensively inquire of enlightened masters. 7. Constantly rely upon [the teachings].

Virtuous Friend, it is difficult to attain the subtle essence of this school; you must apply yourself with meticulous care. Within this, one may suddenly awaken to the True Cause, which is precisely the gradual stage for transcending the mundane world.
The school is the Chan school. "Wondrous" refers to matters upon the edge of a sword, walking upon the edge of an icicle;
it is the great function where heaven revolves and the total capacity that unrolls like lightning. Apply yourself with meticulous care; by all means, avoid being reckless.
Suddenly awaken to the Nirvana of the Three Virtues within the cause, and emerge into the Nirvana of the Three Virtues within the fruit beyond the mundane world.

This then destroys the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms. One comes to know that all internal and external phenomena are entirely unreal, arising through transformations of the mind, and are all merely provisional designations.

The three realms consist of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*). These are: the four continents; the four evil destinies; the six heavens of the desire realm; the Brahma-king heaven; the four dhyānas;
the four formless attainments; the heaven of non-conception; and the five [levels] of the *anāgāmin*. Because cause and effect do not cease, they are called "existence.

All internal and external phenomena—whether within the realms or outside the realms—are the blazing flames of affliction; fundamentally, they are not real dharmas, but arise through the transformations of the mind.

In this regard, the beginning and the end support one another, and the subjective and the objective are in harmony; being neither identical nor different, they establish the phenomena of defilement and purity within the world.
Therefore it is said: "Birth and death arise from consciousness and mind; no sentient beings can be found. Ascension and descent belong to causes and conditions."
There is no real self to be found;
do not direct the mind toward it for attachment. Simply let the emotions not cling to objects, and how could objects obstruct the person?

Let the Dharma-nature flow freely as it will; neither sever it nor continue it. Hearing sounds and seeing forms are but the ordinary course of life; whether on this side or that, its application is unimpeded.
[Omission]. This section of the text is the *amṛta* (nectar) for saving the world. If one practices in accordance with it, the Way lies herein. It does not require further exertion;
when the mind comes to rest [upon this], it is called the Six-Syllable Vidyārāja. What follows below is nothing other than an elaboration of the text. If a person...

When the mind does not take objects as its conditions, how could the myriad things obstruct a person? An ancient worthy said: "The person of ultimate attainment eliminates the mind but does not eliminate objects;
the foolish person eliminates objects but does not eliminate the mind. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) flows everywhere, termed the "constant flow of the Real.
It cannot be severed, nor can it be continued. Regarding the two lines on hearing sounds: it is like holding the Great Sword (Tà'ā); there is no room for deliberation.
These two lines clarify that when a bright mirror stands upon its stand, it reflects whatever appears before it;

if one’s conduct and stillness are likewise, then one truly does not wear the Dharma robes in vain, but rather repays the four debts of gratitude and delivers beings from the three realms of existence.
"If one can remain non-retrogressive in life after life, the stage of Buddhahood may certainly be expected.
This section follows from what preceded it. These two phrases refer to self-benefit, and these two phrases likewise refer to the benefit of others.

In the cultivation of the mind, only non-retrogression is valued; this is termed *avaivartika* (non-retrogression). As for "the stage of Buddhahood," it refers to the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*bhūmi*).
The wondrous awakening of awakening is the sequence of stages for the practice of ancient Buddhas, distinct and orderly without confusion.
As guests traveling through the three realms, they appear and disappear to serve as models for others. This single study is most wondrous and most profound.
Simply discern a heart of resolve, and you will certainly not be deceived.
This clarifies that for one who cultivates the Way, although there is coming and going within the three realms, it is just like being a guest.
First, one is leisurely and self-reliant; second, one establishes the rules for others. This is what is meant by "mysterious beyond the mysterious" and the "multitude of wonders."
This gate depends solely upon one’s own sincere acceptance. How could the Buddha-dharma ever deceive people?
For those of superior faculties, it is taught exclusively for their benefit; for those of middling faculties, a separate method is opened.
If there are those of middling capacity who are unable to transcend all at once, they should for the time being devote their minds to the teachings and study the palm-leaf manuscripts.

As the fortunes of the Dharma decline, those of middling faculties become numerous; such individuals should immediately engage in Chan meditation and the study of the Way to achieve sudden awakening to the profound mechanism of reality.
The teachings consist of the Tripitaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. In the Western lands, they are written on palm leaves; here in this land, they are inscribed upon bamboo and silk.
One must thoroughly investigate their principles and meanings, transmitting and proclaiming them to guide future generations and repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Thus, time shall not be wasted in vain. By upholding these through one's conduct and deportment, one becomes a true vessel of the Dharma within the Sangha.

The first line concerns benefiting oneself; the second line concerns benefiting others. Lines three and four state that to offer this profound mind to the lands of all dust-motes is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Lines five and six refer to being a master of the Dharma; lines seven and eight refer to being a master of the Vinaya.
As for "vessels of the Dharma," these are the finest vessels among the treasures of the Buddha-dharma, like the precious jade *hu* and *lian*.
Have you not seen the climbing vine that winds around a pine tree? It soars to a height of a thousand *xun*. Only by relying on this superior cause can it bring about vast benefit.

The pine tree is a metaphor for the Buddha’s principle; the vine is a metaphor for the student. One *zhang* is called a *xun*. By relying on this most excellent cause, one is able to benefit in accordance with the most excellent fruit.

Diligently cultivate the fast and the precepts; do not allow them to be neglected or transgressed. In life after life and birth after birth, there will be extraordinary and wondrous causes and effects:
first, I exhort you to maintain the fast, never to be deficient; second, I exhort you to maintain the precepts, never to overstep them. Such is the cause.
Such fruits do not pertain to a single lifetime or a single world alone; one shall eternally enjoy extraordinary, sublime, and inexhaustible retribution.

One must not pass the days in negligence or spend time in dull stagnation. It is a pity that this precious time is wasted without seeking spiritual advancement, thereby merely squandering the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions and failing the four debts of gratitude.
As these accumulations deepen, the dust of the mind easily becomes obstructed at every turn.
One becomes stagnant and is held in contempt by others.

The preceding section exhorted practice; this section provides earnest exhortation. If one thus remains negligent and self-abandoning, becoming dejected and failing to exert oneself, one will bring shame upon the patrons who provided sustenance and the practitioners who shed their blood and sweat.
As the long-accumulated burdens increase ever more, they become a defilement upon the mind.
The channels become obstructed; phenomena no longer flow through one another, and everyone looks down upon them with contempt.
As it was said of old: "Since he is a man of great capacity, so am I; one should not disparage oneself or succumb to despondency. If one does not act in this way, [the path will remain closed].

To remain merely within the gates of the monastic community (*śramaṇa*) and let one’s life pass away in vain without deriving any particular benefit—this is what is meant by the ancient saying: "He is a man, and I am a man. This refers to Śākyamuni and Maitreya;

they were none other than ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who were able to establish their resolve. Since you have entered the Dharma-gate, you ought to seek its benefits and strive for spiritual progress.
Exhortation. Hereafter, I urge you once more with renewed earnestness:
I humbly hope that you will arouse a resolute will and open a magnanimous mind. Let your conduct be modeled after those of the superior class;
do not recklessly follow the vulgar and base.

"Decisive and fierce" means having a resolute and intense will. "Penetratingly direct" means being expansive and magnanimous. "Superior stream" refers to those of the highest faculties and sharp aspirations.
"Vulgar and base" refers to those who are commonplace, vulgar, and defiled.

In this present life, you must reach a definitive resolution. It is clear that this cannot be left to others; you must quiet your intentions and forget all conditions, refraining from opposing the various sensory objects.
When the mind is empty and the environment is still, it is only because you have long been obstructed and unable to pass through.
In this life, one need not wait for a future life; as for the individual, the decision rests entirely with oneself.

First, the cessation of thought and forgetting of sensory dust is taught in contrast to ordinary people. Second, the state of empty stillness that has long stagnated refers to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Read these texts frequently and at all times; use them to admonish yourself, firmly establish yourself as the master, and do not follow worldly sentiments. You are being led by the results of your karma.
It is truly difficult to evade. As sound is harmonized by its echo and form is made upright by its shadow, the sequence of cause and effect is unmistakable;
how could one not feel anxiety and dread? Therefore, I urge you to read this entire chapter thoroughly and to constantly admonish and exhort yourself.

Should you encounter adverse circumstances, strive to maintain self-mastery. If there are matters that arise, do not follow worldly sentiments. When the fruits of future karma ripen, try to see who will be the one to experience them.
Who receives [the retribution]? It is like an echo conditioned by sound, or like a shadow manifested from a form. Regarding such causes and effects, how can one not feel a chill in one's heart?

Thus the Sūtra says: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish; when the conditions and causes meet, the fruit of retribution returns to be experienced by oneself."
Regarding the retribution of causes and conditions: when the Buddha was in the world, King Prasenajit, having newly ascended the throne, sought a marriage alliance with the Śākya clan of Kapilavastu.
At that time, a daughter born to Mahānāma’s maidservant, who was of upright and beautiful countenance, was sent to King Prasenajit.
Later, she gave birth to a son named Virūḍhaka. When he reached the age of eight, he was—
The son of the brahmin Bhāradvāja went to the kingdom of the Śākyas. The Śākyas had recently constructed a lecture hall, intending to invite the Buddha to offer him hospitality.
When Vimalakīrti (Liu-li) arrived at the hall, he immediately ascended the lion Dharma-seat.
The Śākyas reviled him, saying, "This offspring of a slave girl dares to enter here and sit! Vimalakīrti harbored resentment and said to Bhāradvāja, "These Śākyas have disparaged me."
Having reached this point, wait until you have become king; then you must inform me. When Devadatta ascended the throne, he was filled with malice and informed [the king] of the previous events.

He assembled an army and went forth to wage war, utterly exterminating the Śākya clan. Ānanda, overcome with grief and suffering, informed the Buddha. At that very moment, the Tathāgata suffered from a headache.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "In the past, there was a fishing village in this city. The people within the city all engaged in fishing."
Fish-eaters. In a pond there were two kinds of fish: the first was called *piṣṭa* (flour), and the second was called *bahujihva* (many-tongued). Each harbored a grudge for the other.
At that time, a young boy was on the bank; seeing the fish leaping about, he was delighted and struck one of the fish on the head with a stick.
At that time, the people of the city of Roruka were the Śākyas of today; the fish *Pūya* was Rāhula;
the fish *Bahujihva* was Bhadrika; and the young boy was my own self.
Therefore, know that the punishments of the three realms entangle and kill one; strive with diligence in cultivation and do not let the days pass in vain.

Only by deeply understanding the faults and afflictions can one truly exhort others to practice and uphold the Dharma. May we, throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, always be fellow practitioners of the Dharma wherever we may be.
Criminal punishment is the retribution of karma; entanglement is that which is experienced. It depends solely upon diligent cultivation to attain liberation from all sufferings.
The Great Master himself spoke thus, for he deeply understood the faults and afflictions of delusive habits; only then did he use words and writing to exhort one another. From this day forward...
If one is willing to practice and uphold [this teaching], then in every land and at every dust mote, one shall become a true companion on the Path.
Thus, he composed this inscription:

An inscription (*ming*) is a record (*zhi*). In antiquity, vessels such as basins, bowls, stools, and desks all had records and inscriptions; these were used from time to time as reminders to encourage self-reflection.
Examine and restrain [yourself].
This illusory body is like a dream-house; its objects are as empty as space. Its prior limit is infinite; how could its subsequent limit ever be reached?
The four great elements form this illusory body, and the three realms constitute this dream-house. Like objects in the sky, they falsely appear and are thus established.

Regarding form (*rūpa*): the past constitutes the prior limit, wherein one has already undergone endless suffering; the future constitutes the subsequent limit, wherein how could one ever achieve success?
Since the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) has not yet opened, this is truly no minor matter.
Emerging here and submerging there, rising and sinking until utterly exhausted, one cannot yet escape the three wheels; when will there be rest? The first phrase:
emerging and submerging endlessly between this land and that realm. The second phrase: wandering and returning without end between heaven and the human world.
The third phrase: still unable to escape the saṃsāra of the three realms of existence. The fourth phrase: ultimately, when will there be rest? (Exhausting the capacity of speech.)
I exhort you: each person must exert their own effort.
Clinging to the world, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) form a substantial body through latent conditions. From birth until old age, one gains nothing at all.
That sentient beings cling to the three periods of time is entirely because the five aggregates act as conditions to produce this illusory substance. Where there is birth, there must inevitably...
There is old age; where there is old age, there must be death. Thus, throughout one's entire life, what is gained?
It is like a thief entering an empty house; one must go there in person.
Fundamental ignorance: because of this, one is deluded.

The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because it relies upon the ālayavijñāna, it is said that there is non-awakening due to ignorance, which gives rise to the capacity for seeing, the capacity for manifestation, and the grasping of objects;
it gives rise to the continuity of thought. Therefore, it is said that one is deluded."
Time is precious; a single moment is unpredictable. If this life passes in vain, the next will be obstructed.
One must cherish time in the present, for human life exists in every instant. If one does not cultivate the Way in this life, the next birth will remain blocked by hindrances.
By examining the fruit, one knows the cause; once the cause is clarified, the fruit will naturally become wholesome.
From delusion to delusion, all is due to the six thieves. One wanders through the six realms and crawls about within the three worlds.
As the Sutra says: "Once deluded, one takes this as the mind; one is certain to be confused, regarding it as being within the physical body.

This is what is meant by "a person who is doubly deluded," revolving without end. The "six thieves" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which plunder the family treasure. "Crawling about" describes the manner of stumbling and faltering.
Visit an enlightened teacher early on and draw near to those of high virtue. Discern the nature of body and mind to clear away the thorns.
A good spiritual friend provides the first word of instruction; a good spiritual friend who practices together provides the second word.
Discern the three actions of the body and the three of the mind to clear away the thorns, thereby nurturing the sprout of spiritual awakening.

The world is inherently floating and empty; how could the manifold conditions ever constrain one? One must investigate and exhaustively study the principles of the Dharma, taking awakening as the standard.
All phenomena in the world are but floating and insubstantial; it is merely that the mind does not cling to things—how could things themselves force themselves upon the person?
It lies solely in the diligent investigation and thorough inquiry into the subtle principles of all dharmas, until one reaches great penetration and great awakening; this is the rule.
Both mind and objects are cast aside; do not record, do not recall. The six sense faculties are serene; walking and standing are tranquil.

As for the mind and the six consciousnesses, the objects and the six sensory realms—recording the present and recollecting the past and future—one is serene, possessing the appearance of self-attainment.
"Walking and standing" refers to the four modes of deportment. The mind is thus tranquil and the mouth is silent; the three karmas are pure, and there is no effort.
The merit of this is such that the profound Way can be realized by those capable of it.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas all cease.
The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena. When both light and objects are forgotten, what else remains? As Ratnakūṭa says:
The bodhicitta is fundamentally without name or verbal expression; the mind and sentient beings are likewise so.
Within this, even the bodhisattva cannot be apprehended; this is called the bodhicitta. That all phenomena are simultaneously stilled—this is it.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in the stage of the equality of emptiness, they do not perceive parents, sisters, children, kinsmen, friends, or those who are enemies or neutral.
They do not even perceive the aggregates, elements, or sense bases, nor sentient beings or a life-span.
Just as space has no father, mother, brother, wife, or child, so too all phenomena—apart from what is called "mind"—do not exist externally.
Dharma. Outside of Dharma, there is no mind. When the mind arises, all manner of dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of dharmas cease.
When the one mind does not arise, it is as stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*: "If a person’s mind is not deluded, they are a Bodhisattva in this very life.

If you practice according to this, you will transcend the three realms, break free from the cage, and achieve Buddhahood and become a Patriarch as easily as pointing at something in the palm of your hand.
The Admonition of Chan Master Taoyuan of Mount Gui (Concluded)
